The electricity trade transformed from Nepal importing power to becoming a net exporter to India during monsoon season. Agreements for long-term power purchase contracts advanced the sector.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; project compliance requirements
exceptions: Environmental impact assessment requirements
Community benefit sharing mandates

quiz.q: What has changed in Nepal's electricity relationship with India?
options: Nepal still imports all power from India
Nepal became a net power exporter to India during monsoon
Nepal and India have no energy ties
quiz.explanation: Nepal transformed from an electricity importer to a net hydropower exporter to India during monsoon season as major hydropower projects came online.

laws.title: Migrant Worker Rights and Kafala Reform
laws.subtitle: Nepal Protects Workers in Gulf Countries
laws.fullDescription: Nepal, one of the largest migrant worker sending countries, negotiated improved protections for Nepali workers in Gulf states, including salary guarantees, right to change employers, and repatriation funds. Nepal leveraged its skilled worker supply to push for reforms to the kafala sponsorship system that tied workers to employers.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for illegal recruitment agencies; contract enforcement
exceptions: Bilateral labor agreement compliance
Government insurance fund for workers abroad

quiz.q: What system in Gulf states did Nepal push to reform to protect its migrant workers?
options: Kafala sponsorship system that tied workers to employers
quiz.explanation: Nepal pushed for reforms to the kafala sponsorship system in Gulf states, which tied workers to their employers and limited their ability to change jobs or leave.

laws.title: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Risk
laws.subtitle: Nepal Monitors GLOF Threats From Climate Change
laws.fullDescription: Nepal faced growing risk from glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) as climate change melted Himalayan glaciers faster. New glacial lakes formed and grew, threatening mountain communities and critical infrastructure. Nepal developed early warning systems with Swiss and other international technical assistance.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; disaster preparedness requirements
exceptions: Emergency evacuation authority
International early warning network

quiz.q: What does GLOF stand for in Nepal's climate risk context?
quiz.explanation: GLOF stands for Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, a growing risk in Nepal as climate change creates new glacial lakes that can catastrophically breach and flood downstream communities.

laws.title: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods and Climate Vulnerability
laws.subtitle: Nepal faces catastrophic flood risk as Himalayan glaciers melt
laws.fullDescription: Nepal has over 3,000 glacial lakes, and climate change is causing many to grow dangerously large. Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) can release millions of cubic meters of water in minutes, destroying downstream communities. The 2023 Sikkim GLOF killed hundreds. Nepal is installing early warning systems and draining some lakes artificially. Hydropower projects also face risks from glacial floods. Climate change is fundamentally reshaping Nepal's geography and disaster risk.
laws.penalty: Construction in GLOF flood plains requires hazard assessment and early warning connectivity
exceptions: Emergency evacuation infrastructure bypasses normal permitting
Traditional settlements in historic locations receive relocation assistance rather than penalties

laws.title: Himalayan Tourism Overcrowding and Permit Reform
laws.subtitle: Everest faces crowding crisis as Nepal reforms climbing permits
laws.fullDescription: Mount Everest has become dangerously overcrowded with hundreds of climbers attempting summits simultaneously, creating deadly bottlenecks in the 'death zone.' Nepal earns significant revenue from climbing permits ($11,000 per person) but faces pressure to limit numbers for safety. 2023 saw record summits but also controversy over unrealistic permit quotas. Nepal is reforming permit systems to require experience certification and is raising permit prices. The climbing economy is central to Nepal's tourism revenue.
laws.penalty: Climbing without proper permits and certified guides is prohibited and enforced on mountain approaches
exceptions: Scientific research expeditions receive separate permit category
Search and rescue operations have emergency access provisions

laws.title: Hydropower Export Potential and India Energy Partnership
laws.subtitle: Nepal sells electricity to power-hungry India from Himalayan rivers
laws.fullDescription: Nepal has enormous hydropower potential — 83,000 MW theoretically, 40,000+ MW practically feasible — from its Himalayan rivers. The country has begun exporting electricity to India under long-term agreements. The Upper Tamakoshi (456 MW) and other projects are transforming Nepal from electricity importer to exporter. India's growing energy demand and Nepal's surplus potential create a natural partnership. China also invests in Nepalese hydropower, creating geopolitical competition. Hydropower revenue could transform Nepal's economy.
laws.penalty: Foreign hydropower investment requires government approval; projects near international borders have security review requirements
exceptions: Run-of-river small hydro projects under 5 MW have simplified licensing
Community micro-hydro installations in remote areas receive government subsidies

quiz.q: How much of Nepal's theoretically feasible hydropower potential has been developed?
quiz.explanation: Nepal has developed less than 10% of its feasible hydropower potential despite having 40,000+ MW available — making hydropower export to India a transformative economic opportunity.

laws.title: Mount Everest Permit Revenue and Summit Congestion
laws.subtitle: Nepal earns millions from Everest permits while managing deadly crowding
laws.fullDescription: Nepal earns approximately $5 million annually from Everest climbing permits. The 2019 season saw horrific congestion photos — hundreds of climbers queued in the death zone, contributing to deaths. Nepal imposed stricter requirements: guides must have summited Everest twice, climbers must have summited another 8,000m peak first. Despite these requirements, commercial operators push inexperienced clients. The 2023 season saw record summits (657) but also deaths. Nepal balances revenue from permits with safety and environmental responsibility.
laws.penalty: Climbing without required permits and certified guides carries equipment confiscation and ban from future permits
exceptions: Reconnaissance and acclimatization expeditions have different permit requirements than summit attempts
Scientific research expeditions receive fee waivers in exchange for research data sharing

quiz.q: How much does Nepal earn annually from Everest climbing permits?
quiz.explanation: Nepal earns approximately $5 million annually from Everest climbing permits at $11,000 each — significant revenue for a poor country, but raising questions about how many permits to sell given deadly crowding in the death zone.

laws.title: Everest Overcrowding and Mountain Tourism Management
laws.subtitle: Nepal managing the commercialization of the world's highest peak
laws.fullDescription: Mount Everest and Nepal's other Himalayan peaks generate critical tourism revenue for one of Asia's poorest countries, but overcrowding has created safety, environmental, and ethical problems. The death zone traffic jam images from 2019 — with hundreds of climbers queuing near the summit in dangerous thin air — sparked global concern. Nepal issues over 300 permits annually at $11,000 each, generating significant revenue but creating crowding blamed for deaths. The mountain faces severe pollution requiring expensive cleanup expeditions. Nepal has debated raising permit fees, limiting total permits, and requiring experience prerequisites. Nepal also faces hydropower development potential, and remittances from Nepali workers abroad are a major economic pillar.
laws.penalty: Climbing without permits carries serious legal consequences; littering on mountains carries fines
exceptions: Search and rescue operations have emergency access provisions

quiz.q: What caused global alarm about Everest in 2019?
options: Images of hundreds of climbers in a dangerous death zone traffic jam
Discovery that Sherpa guides were being exploited
A glacier collapse blocking the main climbing route
quiz.explanation: Images of a massive queue of climbers in the death zone near Everest's summit in 2019 caused global alarm, raising questions about Nepal's permit system and mountain management.

laws.title: Political Instability and Coalition Government Cycling
laws.subtitle: Nepal's chronic governance crisis amid development challenges
laws.fullDescription: Nepal has had over 30 governments since transitioning to a federal democratic republic in 2008, reflecting extreme political fragmentation and instability. Coalition governments typically last months before collapsing, with parties switching allegiances for ministerial positions. This instability has hampered economic development — Nepal requires massive infrastructure investment for hydropower, roads, and tourism, but project implementation suffers under governments that change before completing initiatives. Nepal has significant hydropower potential that could transform the economy through electricity exports to India, but development has been slow. The communist parties (CPN-UML and CPN-Maoist Centre) and Nepali Congress have alternated in various coalitions. Nepal has also been navigating between India (its primary economic partner) and China (growing economic presence through BRI infrastructure).
laws.penalty: Corruption is prosecuted under anti-corruption laws; political violence carries criminal penalties
exceptions: Coalition governments often provide informal protections for allied politicians

quiz.q: Approximately how many governments has Nepal had since transitioning to a federal democratic republic in 2008?
quiz.explanation: Nepal has had over 30 governments since becoming a federal democratic republic in 2008 — reflecting extreme political fragmentation that has hampered development and infrastructure investment.

laws.title: Glacier Melt and Himalayan Water Crisis
laws.subtitle: Nepal's mountains losing ice at alarming rates
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Himalayan glaciers are melting at accelerating rates due to climate change, with some studies showing 2°C warming in the region. This creates short-term glacial lake outburst flood risks and long-term water security threats for hundreds of millions downstream in the Ganges and Brahmaputra basins. Nepal has established early warning systems for glacial lake outburst floods but funding for comprehensive adaptation remains inadequate. Nepal argues its carbon footprint is negligible while bearing enormous climate costs.
laws.penalty: High-altitude construction requires glacial impact assessment; no specific penalties for glacier melt itself
exceptions: Scientific expeditions have special access to restricted glacier zones
Hydroelectric development under environmental review incorporates glacier projections
laws.sourceLabel: Nepal Ministry of Forests and Environment

quiz.q: What downstream risk do Himalayan glacier melt and glacial lakes pose?
quiz.explanation: Glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) are a major immediate risk from glacier melt, while long-term water security threats affect hundreds of millions downstream in the Ganges and Brahmaputra basins.

laws.title: Political Instability Revolving Door
laws.subtitle: Nepal's constitution cannot produce stable governments
laws.fullDescription: Nepal has had over a dozen governments in the decade since adopting its 2015 constitution. Coalition governments form and collapse with remarkable frequency as smaller parties extract concessions and switch sides. KP Sharma Oli and Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda) have each served multiple terms with party switches. The instability has hampered development, earthquake reconstruction and economic growth. Nepal sits strategically between India and China, which both exercise influence over Nepali politics.
laws.penalty: No-confidence motions legally permissible; Nepali constitution limits dissolution of parliament in some circumstances
exceptions: President has limited role in government formation under constitutional provisions
Election Commission manages transition periods between governments

quiz.q: How many governments has Nepal had in the decade since adopting its 2015 constitution?
quiz.explanation: Nepal has had over a dozen governments in the decade since adopting its 2015 constitution, with coalition governments forming and collapsing with remarkable frequency as smaller parties switch allegiances—hampering development and governance.

laws.title: Digital Economy and Remittance Technology
laws.subtitle: Nepal's diaspora economy goes digital through fintech
laws.fullDescription: Nepal receives remittances equivalent to about 25% of GDP—one of the highest ratios in the world—primarily from migrant workers in Gulf countries, Malaysia, India and elsewhere. Fintech has transformed how remittances are sent, with digital platforms dramatically reducing costs compared to traditional money transfer operators. Nepal's central bank has encouraged digital financial services. Domestic digital payment platforms are growing. The tech sector is small but growing, with Kathmandu-based startups serving domestic and diaspora markets.
laws.penalty: Money transfer operators must be licensed by Nepal Rastra Bank; remittances must go through formal channels
exceptions: Small informal transfers between family members in practice tolerated though technically regulated
Mobile banking agents in rural areas have simplified operations

quiz.q: What percentage of Nepal's GDP comes from remittances from migrant workers abroad?
quiz.explanation: Nepal receives remittances equivalent to about 25% of GDP—one of the world's highest ratios—primarily from migrant workers in Gulf countries, Malaysia and India, making fintech for remittance transfer critically important for the Nepali economy.

laws.title: Mount Everest Permit Economy
laws.subtitle: Nepal earns millions from trekking and climbing permits
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Himalayan mountains, including Everest, Annapurna and others, generate significant tourism and permit revenue. The government charges $11,000 per person for an Everest summit permit. Over-crowding on Everest has created dangerous conditions with bottlenecks near the summit and disputes over limiting permits. Nepal earns significant government revenue from mountaineering fees and trekking permits. Climate change is threatening glaciers and altering conditions on the mountains that Nepal's tourism depends on.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized climbing or trekking in permit-required areas subject to fines and deportation
exceptions: Nepali nationals have different permit requirements than foreign climbers
Search and rescue operations can proceed without normal permit requirements

quiz.q: How much does Nepal charge per person for an Everest summit permit?
quiz.explanation: Nepal charges $11,000 per person for a Mount Everest summit permit, with popular peaks generating millions in government revenue—though over-crowding has created dangerous conditions and calls to limit the number of permits issued.

laws.title: National Climate Change Policy and NDC
laws.subtitle: Himalayan Glaciers and Mountain Ecosystem
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's National Climate Change Policy targets carbon neutrality by 2045 and 15% emissions reduction by 2030. Nepal is at the forefront of climate impacts: Himalayan glaciers are melting, reducing dry-season river flows, increasing glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), and threatening water security for hundreds of millions downstream. Mount Everest is warming and losing ice faster. Nepal committed to generating 15,000 MW of electricity from renewable (mostly hydro) by 2030. Nepal has also established the REDD+ framework for forest carbon payments.
laws.penalty: National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act; fines for poaching and habitat destruction; criminal penalties
exceptions: Indigenous communities' traditional forest use
High-altitude pilgrimage activities

laws.title: Nepal Free Health Services and Insurance Scheme
laws.subtitle: Healthcare in the Himalayas
laws.fullDescription: Nepal provides free basic health services through government health facilities, including delivery services, family planning, and essential medicines. Nepal's National Health Insurance Program covers about 25% of the population, expanding annually. Nepal has achieved significant health progress despite being one of Asia's poorest countries — child mortality and maternal mortality have dropped dramatically. Nepal faces unique healthcare challenges: extreme geographic isolation requiring helicopter and porter transport for remote Himalayan communities; altitude sickness; and the 2015 Gorkha earthquake killed 9,000 and damaged health infrastructure. Nepal also has significant mental health challenges post-earthquake and among migrant workers.
laws.penalty: Health facility standards enforced; drug quality control; criminal liability for malpractice
exceptions: Traditional Ayurvedic and Tibetan medicine practitioners under separate licensing
Community health volunteers operate under simplified framework

laws.title: Nepal Foreign Employment Act and Remittance Economy
laws.subtitle: Migrant Workers and the Gulf Connection
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Foreign Employment Act regulates labor migration, which is central to Nepal's economy — approximately 1,500 Nepalis leave for foreign employment daily, primarily to Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Malaysia, and Kuwait. Remittances account for ~25% of Nepal's GDP, the third-highest ratio globally. The kafala (sponsorship) system in Gulf states ties workers to employers, creating vulnerability to abuse. Nepal has banned workers from going to certain countries after deaths, and negotiated 'free visa, free ticket' policies with some destinations. Nepal's domestic workers — also legally protected under law — are mostly rural women.
laws.penalty: Illegal recruitment: criminal prosecution; foreign employment companies: license revocation; labor rights violations abroad: diplomatic intervention
exceptions: Informal labor migration continues despite regulations
Domestic workers under separate legal framework

laws.title: School Sector Development Plan
laws.subtitle: Nepal's federal education restructuring
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's School Education Act and School Sector Development Plan restructured education following the 2015 constitution's federal system, devolving education management to local governments. Nepal provides free basic education (Grades 1-8) and free secondary education (Grades 9-12). Despite progress—literacy rose from 54% (2001) to 76% (2021)—challenges persist: remote mountain schools, multi-grade teaching, brain drain of teachers, and earthquake damage recovery. Nepal's SEE (Secondary Education Examination) replaced the old SLC 'Iron Gate' exam.
laws.penalty: Local governments failing to maintain minimum school standards face provincial oversight; schools without certified teachers face corrective action plans
exceptions: Community schools receive additional government support
Monasteries and gurukuls provide alternative religious education

quiz.q: What replaced Nepal's notorious 'Iron Gate' SLC exam for Grade 10 students?
quiz.explanation: The SEE (Secondary Education Examination) replaced the old School Leaving Certificate (SLC) exam in 2016-17, which was dubbed the 'Iron Gate' due to its high failure rates. The SEE uses grade-based assessment rather than the binary pass/fail of the SLC.

laws.title: Foreign Employment Act and Qatar/Gulf Deaths
laws.subtitle: Nepal's labor export crisis and worker deaths
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Foreign Employment Act (2007) regulates one of the world's most migration-dependent economies — remittances represent 25%+ of Nepal's GDP. An estimated 3.5 million Nepalis work abroad, primarily in Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, and Kuwait. The 2022 FIFA World Cup brought attention to deaths of Nepalese construction workers in Qatar — estimated at 6,500+ over a decade under the kafala (sponsorship) system. Nepal has banned women under 40 from working as domestic workers in Gulf states due to abuse. The Foreign Employment Promotion Board manages worker welfare.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed recruitment agencies (manpower companies) face criminal charges; those charging excessive fees from workers face prosecution; fraudulent job offers for foreign employment are a criminal offense
exceptions: Nepalese going for study or skilled professional work have different permits
Gulf countries with labor agreements receive certified worker protection

quiz.q: Nepal's remittances from overseas workers represent approximately what percentage of its GDP?
quiz.explanation: Nepal has one of the world's highest remittance-to-GDP ratios at approximately 25-30%, making it extremely dependent on overseas worker earnings. This dependence creates pressure to send workers abroad even when labor conditions in destination countries are dangerous or exploitative.

laws.title: Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act
laws.subtitle: Nepal's drug law in cannabis-rich Himalayan region
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act criminalizes drug trafficking and use. Nepal has a unique cultural relationship with cannabis — bhang and charas (resin) have been used in religious contexts for millennia (particularly in Shiva worship) and Nepal's Himalayan regions are known for high-quality cannabis. Nepal criminalized cannabis in 1976 under US pressure. There have been movements to re-legalize cannabis for tourism and revenue, though reforms have not been enacted. Nepal faces heroin transit from India and domestically produced cannabis trafficking.
laws.penalty: Cannabis possession for personal use: 3-18 months; cannabis trafficking: 5-10 years; hard drug trafficking: 5-20 years; repeat trafficking: up to life imprisonment; drug use of foreigners: deportation
exceptions: Religious use of bhang and cannabis in Hindu ceremonies traditionally tolerated
Foreign tourists caught with small cannabis amounts typically face fines and deportation
Medical narcotics available by prescription

quiz.q: Nepal criminalized cannabis in 1976 largely due to pressure from which country?
quiz.explanation: Nepal criminalized cannabis in 1976 largely due to pressure from the United States as part of the global 'War on Drugs' promoted by the Nixon administration. Previously, Nepal had cannabis shops and was a destination for hippie tourism partly due to legal hashish access.

laws.title: Pioneer in Asia — Supreme Court Ruling for Marriage Equality
laws.subtitle: Nepal's Supreme Court ordered marriage equality registration in 2023
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Supreme Court issued a landmark interim order in November 2023 directing the government to begin registering same-sex marriages. Nepal had already been a regional pioneer, having recognized a third gender (others) on government documents since 2007 and in the constitution since 2015. Nepal decriminalized homosexuality in 2007. Same-sex couples began registering marriages under the Supreme Court order, though permanent legislation is still being formalized. Nepal is one of the most progressive countries in Asia on LGBTQ+ rights.
laws.penalty: Discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; hate crime protections exist under law
exceptions: Implementation of marriage registration is ongoing pending finalized legislation

quiz.q: What pioneering step did Nepal take regarding gender recognition as early as 2007?
options: Recognized a third gender on government documents
quiz.explanation: Nepal recognized a third gender ('others') on government documents in 2007, well before same-sex marriage discussions, making it a regional pioneer in gender recognition in Asia.

laws.title: Press Freedom Improvements With Legal Challenges
laws.subtitle: Nepal has improved press freedom since monarchy but information technology laws threaten online journalism
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's constitution (2015) protects freedom of expression and press. Nepal has transformed dramatically from a monarchy with censored press to a republic with active media. Kathmandu has dozens of newspapers, television channels, and radio stations. However, the Electronic Transaction Act and proposed Media Council Act threaten online journalism with vague provisions. Local journalists face pressure from political parties and regional power brokers. Nepal Press Institute and Federation of Nepali Journalists advocate for press rights. Journalist safety in conflict-affected districts remains a concern.
laws.penalty: Electronic Transaction Act can be used against online journalism; criminal defamation provisions apply
exceptions: Post-monarchy press freedom has significantly improved since 2008

quiz.q: What aspect of Nepal's press freedom has improved most dramatically in recent decades?
options: Transition from monarchical censorship to republic press freedom post-2008
quiz.explanation: Nepal's press freedom has improved most dramatically through the transition from a monarchy (which exercised censorship, especially during the royal takeover 2005-2006) to a federal republic in 2008, opening space for a vibrant multi-party media landscape in Kathmandu.

laws.title: Electronic Transactions Act and Social Media Regulation
laws.subtitle: Nepal uses the Electronic Transactions Act against online content and is developing digital policy
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Electronic Transactions Act (ETA, 2008) criminalizes broad online content including material deemed anti-national, contrary to public morality, or threatening to national integrity. The ETA has been used against social media users. Nepal also banned TikTok in November 2023 citing disruption of social harmony, before lifting the ban in August 2024 after platforms agreed to meet with authorities. Nepal is developing a comprehensive digital policy framework. The Department of Information Technology regulates digital services. Nepal's use of social media for political mobilization has been significant.
laws.penalty: ETA: criminal penalties for prohibited online content; TikTok temporarily banned 2023-2024
exceptions: TikTok ban lifted in 2024 after platform negotiations

quiz.q: What social media platform did Nepal ban in November 2023 and then unban in 2024?
quiz.explanation: Nepal banned TikTok in November 2023 citing disruption of social harmony and failure to control inappropriate content. The ban was lifted in August 2024 after TikTok agreed to meet with Nepali authorities — one of several Asian countries that have banned or restricted TikTok.

laws.title: NRB Banking Rules & Remittance Economy Regulations
laws.subtitle: Nepal's central bank manages a remittance-dependent economy with strict FX controls
laws.fullDescription: Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) regulates all commercial banks, development banks, and finance companies under the Nepal Rastra Bank Act 2002. Nepal's economy is one of the world's most remittance-dependent — remittances exceed 25% of GDP, primarily from Nepali workers in Gulf countries, Malaysia, and India. The NRB requires all remittances to come through licensed channels to capture FX. Nepal pegs the Nepalese rupee to the Indian rupee at NPR 1.60 per INR, meaning Nepal's monetary policy largely mirrors India's. The NRB banned cryptocurrency in 2021 under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act. Digital payments are growing through platforms like eSewa and Khalti.
laws.penalty: Crypto transactions: fines and up to 5 years imprisonment under Foreign Exchange Act; unlicensed money transfer: fines up to NPR 100,000 and 3 years imprisonment; banking violations: fines up to NPR 30 million
exceptions: Indian-Nepali border trade uses both currencies informally with NRB tolerance
Licensed remittance companies have streamlined FX conversion rules
Agricultural cooperative societies have modified licensing requirements

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Nepal's GDP comes from remittances sent by workers abroad?
quiz.explanation: Nepal is among the world's most remittance-dependent economies, with remittances exceeding 25% of GDP. Most come from Nepali migrant workers in Gulf countries (Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia), Malaysia, and India.

laws.title: DFTQC Food Safety & Nepal's Himalayan Food Heritage
laws.subtitle: Nepal's food authority manages safety for its diverse traditional mountain foods
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Department of Food Technology and Quality Control (DFTQC) under the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development regulates food safety. Nepal has a diverse food heritage: dal bhat (lentils and rice) is the national staple, accompanied by tarkari (vegetable curry) and achar (pickle). Newari cuisine of the Kathmandu Valley features unique fermented foods. Nepal's Himalayan region produces yak products — yak butter, yak milk cheese, and yak meat — with specific quality standards. Nepal is a growing tea producer (Nepal tea from the Ilam region is increasingly recognized as premium). Food adulteration — particularly in ghee (clarified butter), spices, and honey — is a significant challenge. Street food safety in Kathmandu is a public health concern given heavy domestic and international tourism.
laws.penalty: DFTQC violations: fines up to NPR 5 lakh and imprisonment up to 2 years; food adulteration (ghee, spices): fines and product confiscation; food poisoning at tourist restaurants: civil liability and license suspension
exceptions: Subsistence farmers selling direct at village markets have simplified DFTQC requirements
Traditional fermented Newari foods for community festivals have cultural exemptions
Small tea producers below processing threshold have DFTQC cooperative certification pathways

quiz.q: What unique Himalayan livestock product does Nepal produce that is gaining international recognition?
options: Yak products — yak butter, milk cheese, and meat from yaks herded at high Himalayan altitudes
Himalayan red panda honey (protected — not legal)
quiz.explanation: Yak (Bos grunniens) products are unique to the Himalayan and Tibetan plateau regions. Yak butter (essential for Tibetan butter tea), yak milk cheese, and dried yak meat are produced by herders at altitudes of 3,000-5,500m. These products are gaining international niche market interest as premium Himalayan foods.

laws.title: Nepal Animal Health and Livestock Services Act
laws.subtitle: Nepal bans cow slaughter as constitutional protection
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's animal welfare framework is unique — the cow is the national animal and its slaughter is constitutionally prohibited (a holdover from the Hindu kingdom era, maintained in the 2015 Constitution). Cow slaughter carries up to 12 years imprisonment. Nepal's Animal Health and Livestock Services Act, 1998 (2055 BS) governs livestock welfare and disease control. Companion animal welfare provisions are limited, though Kathmandu has developed animal welfare programs. Nepal has significant stray dog populations and periodic rabies outbreaks. Dog meat is consumed in some ethnic communities. Animal sacrifice (including the Gadhimai festival — the world's largest mass animal sacrifice) is culturally practiced and legally tolerated. Wildlife is protected under the National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act.
laws.penalty: Cow slaughter: up to 12 years imprisonment; other animal welfare violations: fines under livestock act; wildlife violations: 5–15 years imprisonment
exceptions: Water buffalo slaughter is legal (only cow is protected)
Traditional animal sacrifices
Livestock farming
Licensed hunting in specific areas
laws.sourceLabel: Nepal Animal Health and Livestock Services Act 1998

quiz.q: What unique constitutional animal protection exists in Nepal?
options: Monkeys near temples cannot be disturbed
Cow slaughter is constitutionally prohibited with up to 12 years imprisonment
Tigers are given special judicial standing
quiz.explanation: Nepal's constitution (maintaining the tradition from the Hindu kingdom era) prohibits cow slaughter — the cow is the national animal. Killing a cow carries up to 12 years imprisonment, making it one of the most severe animal-specific criminal penalties in the world.

laws.title: Nepal National Civil Code 2017 — Gender-Neutral Marriage Provision
laws.subtitle: Nepal's 2017 code opened door for same-sex marriage
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's National Civil Code 2017 replaced centuries-old laws and included a landmark provision requiring the government to study and potentially recognize same-sex marriage. Nepal's Supreme Court had previously directed the government in 2007 to study same-sex marriage legalization. Nepal's Supreme Court issued an interim order in 2023 directing the government to register same-sex marriages pending a final ruling — making Nepal the first South Asian country to take such a step. Nepal's Civil Code defines marriage as between man and woman but the Supreme Court's direction represents a critical challenge. Nepal has previously allowed gender marker changes on official documents. Divorce: couples can divorce mutually or on specific grounds after 1 year. Property: equal sharing for married couples.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement through district courts and high courts; child support enforced; criminal domestic violence charges
exceptions: Religious personal practices for minority communities
Ethnic customary marriage practices recognized in some contexts
Supreme Court orders override Civil Code for same-sex registration
laws.sourceLabel: Nepal Muluki Dewani Samhita (National Civil Code 2017)

quiz.q: What significant same-sex marriage development occurred in Nepal in 2023?
options: Nepal legalized same-sex marriage by parliament vote
Nepal's Supreme Court issued an interim order directing the government to register same-sex marriages — the first in South Asia
Nepal made same-sex marriage subject to referendum
quiz.explanation: In 2023, Nepal's Supreme Court issued an interim order directing the government to register same-sex marriages while the constitutional question is pending final ruling — making Nepal the first South Asian country to take such a judicial step. This followed a 2007 directive and reflected Nepal's progressive constitution on LGBTQ+ rights.

laws.title: Nepal Muluki Dewani Sanhita & Land Reform
laws.subtitle: Civil code property rights and land ceiling laws
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Muluki Dewani Sanhita (Civil Code 2017) modernized property law, including women's equal inheritance rights. The Land Reform Act (1964) introduced land ceilings (haad) to limit landholdings and redistribute to landless peasants — maximum 25 bighas in Terai, 50 ropanis in hills. The Guthi (socio-religious land trust) system in Kathmandu Valley preserves traditional Newar community property. Nepal's Constitution (2015) guarantees right to property (Art. 25) and requires compensation for acquisition. The Land Use Act (2019) aimed to rationalize land classification and prevent conversion of agricultural land to residential use.
laws.penalty: Excess landholding above ceiling: government acquisition at fixed rate; illegal land conversion: criminal fine
exceptions: Land ceiling: 25 bighas Terai, 50 ropanis hills
Women's equal inheritance rights guaranteed under 2017 Civil Code
laws.source: Muluki Dewani Sanhita 2017; Land Reform Act 1964 (amended)

quiz.q: What important gender-equality change did Nepal's 2017 Civil Code make to property rights?
options: Required women to own 50% of all property
quiz.explanation: Nepal's Muluki Dewani Sanhita (Civil Code 2017) explicitly guaranteed women equal inheritance rights to parental property, a significant reform in a society where customary practices had historically favored sons in inheritance.

laws.title: Nepal Consumer Protection Act 2018
laws.subtitle: Comprehensive consumer rights with enforcement authority
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Consumer Protection Act (2018) replaced the earlier 1998 act with more comprehensive protections including strict liability for defective products, penalties for false advertising, and mandatory labeling in Nepali. The Department of Commerce, Supplies and Consumer Protection (DoCSCP) enforces the law. Nepal has specific rules for food adulteration under the Food Act. Consumer courts and consumer protection offices operate at the district level. Nepal's remote geography creates significant challenges for consumer protection enforcement in rural areas. The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has a separate consumer complaints mechanism for electricity service. The 2018 act for the first time included e-commerce consumer protections.
laws.penalty: Product liability: strict liability for defects; DoCSCP fine: up to NPR 300,000; false advertising: criminal penalty
exceptions: 2018 Act includes first e-commerce consumer protections
Remote geography challenges rural consumer protection enforcement

quiz.q: What was significant about Nepal's Consumer Protection Act 2018 regarding digital commerce?
options: It banned all e-commerce in Nepal
It was the first time Nepal's consumer law included e-commerce protections
It required all e-commerce to be in Nepali language only
quiz.explanation: Nepal's Consumer Protection Act (2018) was the first time Nepal's consumer protection legislation included specific provisions for e-commerce transactions — a significant update recognizing the growth of online shopping even in Nepal's developing market.

laws.title: Constitution of Nepal, 2015
laws.subtitle: Federal democratic republic after monarchy abolished
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's 2015 Constitution transformed Nepal from a unitary Hindu Kingdom (the world's only Hindu state) to a federal secular democratic republic. This came after years of Maoist insurgency (1996-2006, 17,000+ killed), a people's movement, and the abolition of the monarchy (2008). Nepal became federal with 7 provinces (a significant change from a centralized state). The constitution recognized multiple marginalized groups including Dalits, Janajatis (indigenous nationalities), and Madhesi communities (Terai plains peoples). Madhesi protests erupted over perceived under-representation in the constitution — contributing to an Indian border blockade in 2015-16. Nepal's transition from Hindu Kingdom to secular federal republic was one of South Asia's most dramatic constitutional transformations.
laws.penalty: Challenging the democratic republic system: criminal prosecution under law against activities subversive to national integrity.
exceptions: Provinces have constitutional authority over listed subjects in Schedule 6
Indigenous communities have customary rights over natural resources in their territories
Federal parliament has residual powers for unspecified subjects

quiz.q: What unique status did Nepal hold until its 2008 constitutional change?
options: Nepal was the world's only communist monarchy
Nepal was the world's only Hindu Kingdom — the only country with Hinduism as the official state religion
Nepal was the world's only country without a national capital
Nepal was governed by the last remaining hereditary Buddhist theocracy
quiz.explanation: Until King Gyanendra was deposed in 2008 (following the Constituent Assembly election abolishing the monarchy), Nepal was the world's only official Hindu Kingdom — the only country that formally designated Hinduism as the state religion. The new constitution declared Nepal secular, completing a transition from absolute monarchy to constitutional monarchy to republic over 20 years. The change was remarkable: a country that had defined itself by its Hindu royal identity became a secular federal republic.

laws.title: Foreign Employment Act 2007 — Nepal's Labor Migration
laws.subtitle: Nepal's massive overseas labor migration and kafala system abuses
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Foreign Employment Act governs labor migration — one of the world's largest relative to population: 4+ million Nepali workers abroad, primarily in Gulf countries (Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait) and Malaysia. Remittances are ~25% of Nepal's GDP — making Nepal one of the most remittance-dependent economies globally. Nepal's workers in Qatar were central to the FIFA World Cup 2022 controversy: reports of 6,500+ migrant worker deaths in Qatar since winning the World Cup bid in 2010 (official Qatari figure disputed vs. worker origin country records). Nepal suspended labor migration to several countries following worker deaths. The kafala (sponsorship) system traps workers to employers.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent foreign employment recruitment: up to 7 years imprisonment. Charging excessive recruitment fees: criminal prosecution under Foreign Employment Act.
exceptions: Individual workers may travel independently without FEPB approval in some categories
Highly skilled professionals (doctors, IT workers) have facilitated migration pathways
Workers in countries with bilateral agreements (Qatar, UAE, Malaysia) have modified protections

quiz.q: What percentage of Nepal's GDP comes from workers' remittances?
options: About 3% — similar to other South Asian countries
Approximately 25% — making Nepal among the world's most remittance-dependent economies
Over 50% — virtually the entire economy depends on overseas workers
quiz.explanation: Nepal's remittances represent approximately 25% of GDP — one of the highest ratios in the world. With 4+ million Nepali workers abroad (in Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, India), money sent home is the primary driver of Nepal's economy and poverty reduction. This dependence creates vulnerability: when COVID closed Gulf countries to new workers and reduced incomes, Nepal's economy was severely stressed. The dependence also reflects domestic job market failures — Nepal cannot create enough employment at home for its labor force.

laws.title: National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act — Nepal
laws.subtitle: Nepal's conservation success and Himalayan climate change
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act (1973) protects extraordinary biodiversity across elevation gradients from subtropical Terai to 8,848m Everest. Nepal has 12 national parks, 1 wildlife reserve, and 6 conservation areas covering 23% of land. Conservation successes: tiger population doubled (2009-2022, 355 to 355+), rhino population recovered (from 100 to 700+), snow leopard monitoring advancing. Nepal's Chitwan and Sagarmatha national parks are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Climate change threatens Nepal: Himalayan glaciers melting at unprecedented rates (70% of glaciers retreating), affecting water supply for millions downstream in India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and China. GLOF risk is increasing as glacial lakes expand.
laws.penalty: Poaching protected species: up to 15 years imprisonment and NPR200,000 fine. Illegal trading in wildlife products: up to 15 years. Encroachment on national park: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Buffer zones around parks allow limited community resource use with management plans
Indigenous communities with historical ties to park land may have modified access rights
Scientific research permits allow entry to restricted areas with pre-approved protocols
laws.sourceLabel: Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Nepal

quiz.q: What wildlife conservation success has Nepal achieved for tigers and rhinos?
options: Nepal completely eliminated poaching with 100% success since 2010
Nepal doubled its tiger population (2009-2022) and recovered rhinos from 100 to 700+ — significant conservation achievements
Nepal reintroduced tigers and rhinos from India after they became locally extinct
Nepal transferred all tigers and rhinos to sanctuaries in richer countries for better protection
quiz.explanation: Nepal's wildlife conservation is celebrated globally: its tiger population grew from 121 (2009) to 355+ (2022) — more than doubling — through anti-poaching enforcement, habitat management, and community co-existence programs. Nepal also recovered its one-horned rhinoceros from ~100 individuals in the 1960s to 700+ today through Chitwan National Park protections. Nepal achieved 'zero poaching years' for tigers and rhinos multiple times, demonstrating that wildlife recovery is possible with adequate political will and community engagement.

laws.title: Nepal Rastra Bank Act — Central Banking and Remittance Economy
laws.subtitle: Managing Nepal's economy of remittances and hydropower potential
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) Act governs the central bank. Nepal's economy has two defining features: overwhelming remittance dependence (25% of GDP) and vast untapped hydropower potential (83,000 MW theoretical capacity, one of world's highest). Nepal has historically exported surplus power to India and has major development finance from India, China, and multilaterals for hydropower projects. Nepal's geographic position between India and China — called 'sandwiched' — creates both opportunity and constraint. NRB manages remittance policy, inflation (which spikes when remittances fuel consumption without commensurate domestic production), and banking sector development. Nepal has high financial inclusion through cooperatives and microfinance.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed banking: criminal prosecution and fines. Unauthorized foreign exchange transactions: administrative fines. Loan fraud: criminal prosecution under financial fraud laws.
exceptions: Cooperatives below threshold operate under Cooperative Act rather than banking law
Microfinance institutions serving rural poor have modified capital requirements
Informal money changers in tourist areas operate under licensing regime distinct from banks
laws.sourceLabel: Nepal Rastra Bank — Central Bank of Nepal

quiz.q: What is Nepal's untapped natural resource that could transform its economy?
options: Himalayan mineral deposits including rare earth elements
83,000 MW of theoretical hydropower capacity — one of the world's highest — largely undeveloped
Agricultural land that becomes more valuable as Himalayan glaciers create irrigation water
Natural gas fields discovered under the Terai plains
quiz.explanation: Nepal sits in the Himalayas, where glaciers and high-altitude precipitation feed steep rivers descending thousands of meters — creating ideal hydropower conditions. Nepal's theoretical hydropower potential of 83,000 MW is enormous (only China, Russia, and a few others have more). Currently, Nepal develops only about 2,000 MW. Developing this potential through projects like the under-construction Budhi Gandaki (1,200 MW) could transform Nepal from a remittance-dependent economy to a power-exporting economy selling electricity to India's 1.4 billion people. Financing, environmental concerns, and geopolitical dynamics complicate development.

laws.title: Muluki Penal Code 2017 — Nepal's Criminal Law Reform
laws.subtitle: Nepal's comprehensive criminal code including LGBTQ+ progress
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Muluki Penal Code (2017) comprehensively revised criminal law. Notably progressive for South Asia: Nepal's Supreme Court ordered the government to legalize same-sex marriage (2023) — making Nepal potentially the first South Asian country to do so (implementation underway). Nepal's Penal Code does not explicitly criminalize consensual same-sex relations (unlike India's Section 377 history). Nepal issues a 'third gender' citizenship category. However, there are challenges: Dalit discrimination, caste-based discrimination (though criminalized), and violence against women remain significant. Nepal has significant trafficking concerns: Nepali women and girls are trafficked to India and Gulf countries.
laws.penalty: Caste-based discrimination: up to 3 years and NPR30,000 fine. Human trafficking: up to 20 years. Domestic violence: up to 3 years and financial compensation to victim. Rape: up to 15 years (life for rape of under-10).
exceptions: Customary practices of ethnic communities may be considered in cultural defense for minor offenses
Youth (under 18) receive juvenile justice treatment with rehabilitation focus
Consensual adult same-sex relations not explicitly criminalized — Supreme Court has ordered marriage equality

quiz.q: What groundbreaking ruling did Nepal's Supreme Court make on marriage equality?
options: Nepal's Supreme Court rejected marriage equality petitions in 2023
Nepal's Supreme Court ordered the government to legalize same-sex marriage in 2023 — potentially making Nepal the first South Asian country to do so
Nepal legalized same-sex civil unions but not marriage
Nepal criminalized same-sex relations following public referendum
quiz.explanation: Nepal's Supreme Court in November 2023 ordered the government to allow same-sex marriage registration — a landmark ruling in South Asia, where most countries still criminalize or severely restrict LGBTQ+ rights. The ruling directed the government to amend the Civil Code. Nepal already issues third gender citizenship, allows same-sex couples to register as domestic partners, and has some same-sex couple rights. If implemented, Nepal would be the first South Asian country to recognize same-sex marriage — a dramatic contrast with neighboring India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka.

laws.title: Nepal Health Policy — Expanding Universal Health Coverage
laws.subtitle: Healthcare access in a mountainous country with geographic barriers
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's National Health Policy aims to provide universal health coverage in one of the world's most geographically challenging countries. 80%+ of Nepal's population lives in hilly and mountainous terrain accessible only by foot or small aircraft. Telemedicine and trained community health workers (Female Community Health Volunteers, FCHVs) have been essential in reaching remote communities. Nepal has made significant health progress: maternal mortality fell from 548/100,000 (1996) to 151/100,000 (2022), mostly from FCHVs supporting safe delivery and referral. Nepal's constitution makes health a fundamental right. Health insurance is being expanded. Emergency helicopters serve high-altitude medical emergencies and Everest climbers.
laws.penalty: Healthcare facility operating without license: administrative fines and closure. Medical malpractice: civil liability and professional council sanctions. Counterfeit medicines: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Community health volunteers may provide basic services without full clinical license
Telemedicine consultations have modified prescription rules for remote areas
Traditional healers (dhami-jhankri) operate under separate recognition framework
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health and Population Nepal

quiz.q: What community health worker program has been crucial to Nepal's healthcare outreach in remote areas?
options: Nepal deployed military helicopters to deliver medicine to all remote areas
Female Community Health Volunteers (FCHVs) — trained village women providing basic health services — have been essential to Nepal's health progress in mountainous terrain
Nepal built a hospital in every village of 1,000+ people regardless of accessibility
Nepal's monks provide healthcare in remote Buddhist communities
quiz.explanation: Nepal's Female Community Health Volunteer (FCHV) program — over 50,000 trained village women providing basic health education, antenatal care support, family planning advice, and referral — has been credited as a key driver of Nepal's dramatic maternal mortality reduction (548 to 151 per 100,000 from 1996-2022). FCHVs reach communities inaccessible to facilities, serving as a bridge between households and the formal health system. The program is studied globally as a low-cost community health model.

laws.title: Tourism Act Nepal — Everest and Trekking Regulation
laws.subtitle: Managing Himalayan tourism from permit requirements to overcrowding
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Tourism Act governs mountain climbing, trekking, and tourism. Everest climbing permits: $11,000/person for standard routes, generating $3-4M annually. In 2023, Nepal issued 478 permits — the most ever — resulting in dangerous overcrowding, with famous 'traffic jam' photos of hundreds of climbers queued near the summit. 18 climbers died in 2023. Nepal has debated: limiting Everest permits, requiring prior high-altitude experience, and raising permit fees to reduce volumes and increase revenue. Trekking requires TIMS cards (Trekking Information Management System). Tourism is ~8% of GDP but was devastated by COVID. Post-COVID recovery has been strong.
laws.penalty: Climbing without permit: confiscation of equipment and fines. Commercial trekking without licensed guide (required in restricted areas): fines. Wildlife in trekking corridor disturbed: conservation law penalties.
exceptions: Nepal citizens may trek national parks with modified permit requirements
Research expeditions receive modified permit terms
Humanitarian missions (medical, rescue) operate under emergency provisions
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Culture Tourism and Civil Aviation Nepal

quiz.q: What problem did Nepal's record 478 Everest permits in 2023 create?
options: Nepal earned too much permit revenue, triggering IMF classification review
Dangerous overcrowding — hundreds of climbers queuing near the summit in 'traffic jams' — contributed to 18 deaths
Too many foreign climbers meant no spaces for Nepali sherpa-led expeditions
Nepal's Everest base camp ran out of toilet facilities
quiz.explanation: Nepal's 2023 record of 478 Everest permits (plus multiple climbers per permit) created dangerous overcrowding: iconic photos showed hundreds of climbers in a single-file queue near the summit, waiting hours in the death zone where every minute reduces chances of survival. The congestion contributed to 18 deaths. Critics argue Nepal prioritizes revenue ($11,000/permit) over safety, while others note that limiting permits would hurt local economies dependent on climbing tourism. Nepal has debated minimum experience requirements and permit limits but has not implemented them.

laws.title: Climate Change Policy Nepal — Himalayan Water Tower
laws.subtitle: Nepal as Asia's water tower under climate stress
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Climate Change Policy (2011, revised 2019) addresses the country's unique climate vulnerability as both contributor to regional water security and victim of glacier retreat. Nepal's glaciers feed Asia's major rivers (Ganges, Brahmaputra, Indus, Mekong via tributaries) — providing water for 1.65 billion people in South and Southeast Asia. As these glaciers retreat (65-80% of Himalayan glaciers retreating), seasonal water availability for downstream countries will shift: initially more water from increased melting, then long-term reduction. Nepal committed to 15% of electricity from renewables by 2030 (already largely met through hydropower). Nepal is extremely climate-vulnerable despite contributing <0.1% of global emissions.
laws.penalty: Industrial pollution in river catchments: criminal prosecution under Environmental Protection Act. Unauthorized mining of glacial riverbeds: heavy fines and criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Small-scale traditional water use upstream does not require downstream notification
Community irrigation projects below threshold exempt from major EIA requirements
Emergency water access during drought conditions may override normal environmental permits
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Forests and Environment Nepal

quiz.q: How many people depend on rivers fed by Nepal's Himalayan glaciers?
options: About 500 million — primarily in India and Bangladesh
Approximately 1.65 billion people in South and Southeast Asia
Virtually no one — Himalayan rivers are too rocky for irrigation downstream
quiz.explanation: Nepal's Himalayan glaciers and high-altitude watersheds feed the headwaters of major Asian rivers — the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and their tributaries — that ultimately provide water for an estimated 1.65 billion people in South and Southeast Asia. Nepal is often called 'Asia's water tower'. As glaciers retreat due to climate change, the timing and volume of river flows will change significantly — with potentially severe consequences for agriculture, drinking water, and hydroelectric power generation across multiple countries that have no control over the source.

laws.title: Transitional Justice — Nepal's Unresolved Civil War Accountability
laws.subtitle: Accountability for atrocities committed during the Maoist conflict
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Maoist insurgency (1996-2006) resulted in 17,000+ deaths, thousands of disappearances, and widespread torture and displacement by both Maoists and government security forces. The Comprehensive Peace Accord (2006) ended the conflict but established only a weak transitional justice mechanism. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) and Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappearances (CIED) were established in 2014 but have been criticized for lack of independence, inadequate witness protection, and amnesty provisions allowing perpetrators to escape accountability. Nepal's Supreme Court repeatedly found the amnesty provisions unconstitutional, but Parliament has been slow to implement reforms. Many survivors demand accountability while some former Maoists (now in government) resist prosecution.
laws.penalty: Crimes against humanity: no statute of limitations under transitional justice framework. Enforced disappearance: criminal offense under new legislation (2024). Torture: criminal offense.
exceptions: Low-level perpetrators who cooperate with TRC may receive reduced sentences
Non-combatants who facilitated logistics without direct violence participation have modified accountability
Victims may choose restorative justice over prosecution in individual cases
laws.sourceLabel: Nepal Peace Portal — Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction

quiz.q: What has delayed Nepal's transitional justice process for 18+ years after the peace accord?
options: Nepal's lack of any legal framework for prosecuting war crimes
Former Maoists who joined mainstream politics (including serving as Prime Ministers) resist prosecution for conflict-era crimes — creating political barriers to accountability
Nepal's Supreme Court ruled all conflict-era crimes were automatically amnestied
International donors required Nepal to abandon transitional justice as a condition of aid
quiz.explanation: Nepal's transitional justice delay reflects a fundamental political conflict: the former Maoist commanders who led the insurgency have become mainstream political leaders (multiple former Maoists served as Prime Minister). These figures have strong incentives to block accountability for conflict-era crimes for which they bear command responsibility. Combined with security forces reluctant to prosecute their own, and victimized communities still lacking political power, Nepal's transitional justice process has dragged on for nearly two decades with minimal accountability.

laws.title: Nepal Citizenship Act & Identity Politics
laws.subtitle: Citizenship law and discrimination in Nepal
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Citizenship Act has been controversial particularly regarding gender discrimination. Previously, children of Nepali mothers and foreign fathers could not obtain citizenship — only children of Nepali fathers. Nepal's women's rights movement campaigned for equal citizenship transmission rights. The 2015 Constitution improved but did not fully equalize citizenship rights: children born to Nepali mothers may obtain naturalized citizenship (not citizenship by descent) if father is foreign — creating a second-class citizenship category. India-Nepal relations are complicated by open border (almost 2 million Nepalis in India, millions of Indians in Nepal with near-free movement). Nepal's plains (Madhesi) people historically had citizenship documentation challenges due to birth registration gaps.
laws.penalty: Obtaining citizenship through fraud: revocation and criminal prosecution. Employing undocumented foreigners in restricted sectors: fines.
exceptions: Indian nationals may live and work in Nepal under Indo-Nepal Peace and Friendship Treaty (1950) — near-free movement
Tibetan refugees who arrived before 1989 have temporary residence documentation
Foreign spouses of Nepali citizens have expedited naturalization pathway

quiz.q: What gender discrimination existed in Nepal's citizenship law that was partially reformed in 2015?
options: Women could not vote or hold citizenship in Nepal
Children of Nepali mothers and foreign fathers could not obtain citizenship — only children of Nepali fathers — creating gender-unequal citizenship transmission
Married women automatically lost their Nepal citizenship
Foreign women married to Nepali men were denied citizenship rights
quiz.explanation: Nepal's citizenship law historically transmitted citizenship through the father: children of Nepali fathers (regardless of mother's nationality) got citizenship by descent, while children of Nepali mothers and foreign fathers faced barriers. This meant Nepali women who married foreigners could not pass citizenship to their children. Women's rights groups campaigned for equality. The 2015 Constitution partially reformed this — children of Nepali mothers with foreign fathers may get naturalized citizenship (not the higher 'citizenship by descent') — still creating an unequal second tier.

laws.title: Anti-Corruption Act and CIAA — Nepal
laws.subtitle: Corruption challenges in Nepal's political economy
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA) is the constitutional anti-corruption body. Nepal ranks poorly on Corruption Perceptions Index (113th/180 in 2022). Corruption is pervasive at multiple levels: petty corruption in public services (payments for licenses, permits, medical care), political corruption in infrastructure contracts, and grand corruption in natural resource allocation. Nepal's political instability (12 Prime Ministers in 15 years post-2008) creates patronage-based governance. The CIAA has prosecuted civil servants and politicians, but large cases involving politically connected figures are rare. Infrastructure projects (roads, hydropower) are characterized by delays, cost overruns, and contractor fraud.
laws.penalty: Public servant corruption: up to 7 years imprisonment and fine plus recovery. Bribery: up to 5 years. Misuse of public property: up to 10 years. Asset forfeiture available for corruption proceeds.
exceptions: Small gifts of customary value during festivals may not constitute bribery if not linked to official action
Internationally financed projects may have parallel oversight by development bank inspectors reducing CIAA jurisdiction
Diplomatic immunity protects foreign officials from CIAA jurisdiction
laws.sourceLabel: Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority Nepal

quiz.q: How does Nepal's political instability relate to corruption?
options: Political instability has no relationship with corruption — they are separate issues
Frequent government changes (12 PMs in 15 years) create patronage-based governance where officials secure loyalties through resource allocation rather than merit — institutionalizing corruption
Nepal's political stability is excellent and corruption is low
Nepal's corruption is caused entirely by foreign aid mismanagement
quiz.explanation: Nepal's extraordinary political instability — 12 Prime Ministers in the 15 years after the 2008 constitutional change — creates structural corruption: since any government may last only months, officials prioritize distributing resources to secure political loyalty over merit-based governance. Infrastructure contracts become patronage tools; bureaucratic positions are rewarded for political support. This patronage cycle means corruption is not merely individual wrongdoing but a structural feature of how the political system maintains itself. Anti-corruption efforts must address underlying political economy, not just individual cases.

laws.title: Glacier Lake Outburst Floods (GLOF) Risk — Nepal
laws.subtitle: Climate change-induced glacial lake disaster risks in Nepal
laws.fullDescription: Nepal faces increasing Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) risk as Himalayan glaciers retreat. As glaciers melt, water accumulates in glacial lakes dammed by unstable moraines. When these dams fail, catastrophic floods rush down mountain valleys — destroying villages, bridges, roads, and hydropower infrastructure in minutes. Nepal has 3,600+ glacial lakes, with hundreds assessed as potentially dangerous. Major GLOF events: Dig Tsho GLOF (1985) destroyed the Namche hydropower project; Dudh Koshi GLOF would threaten millions downstream. Nepal's 2023 GLOF on the Thame valley destroyed a hydropower project under construction. Climate change is accelerating glacier retreat: 65-70% of Nepal's glaciers retreating. Nepal is establishing GLOF early warning systems.
laws.penalty: Construction in GLOF high-risk zones without Disaster Management Authority clearance: prohibited. Building without flood-risk assessment in river corridors: illegal under Building Permit Rules. Violating GLOF early warning evacuation orders: public safety offense.
exceptions: Emergency reconstruction of critical infrastructure may proceed with expedited environmental review
Traditional irrigation channels in GLOF risk zones may be maintained under community resource rights
Research expeditions to glacial lakes require Department of Hydrology and Meteorology permits
laws.sourceLabel: Department of Hydrology and Meteorology Nepal

quiz.q: What makes GLOF risk in Nepal increasing, and what happened at Thame in 2023?
options: GLOF risk is decreasing because Nepal's glaciers are growing under new snow accumulation
Accelerating glacier retreat (65-70% of glaciers retreating) creates more and larger glacial lakes; the 2023 Thame GLOF destroyed a hydropower project under construction
Nepal has never experienced a GLOF event — the risk is theoretical
GLOFs only occur in winter — summer construction in glacial areas is safe
quiz.explanation: Nepal's accelerating glacier retreat due to climate change creates new glacial lakes and enlarges existing ones — all dammed by unstable moraines that can fail without warning. The 2023 Thame valley GLOF destroyed a hydropower project under construction, setting back Nepal's energy development plans. Nepal's $2+ billion hydropower development portfolio faces increasing GLOF risk as projects are built in high Himalayan valleys. The challenge is building critical infrastructure for Nepal's development while managing a climate risk that is increasing year by year.

laws.title: Labor Act 2017 Nepal — Formal Sector Worker Rights
laws.subtitle: Nepal's revised labor law and persistent informality
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Labor Act 2017 updated labor protections: minimum wages, working hours (8-hour day, 48-hour week), social security, and occupational safety. However, Nepal's informal sector employs 90%+ of workers — covered only nominally. Nepal's Social Security Fund (SSF) attempts to extend contributory benefits to formal workers. A key challenge: 4 million Nepalis work abroad (remitting 25% of GDP) where they face exploitation under the kafala system — but are outside Nepal's Labor Act jurisdiction. Returning migrant workers with injuries or disabilities received inadequate compensation historically. Nepal has bilateral labor agreements with Qatar, UAE, Malaysia, and Japan that theoretically provide minimum protections.
laws.penalty: Minimum wage violations: administrative fines and make-up pay. Failure to contribute to Social Security Fund: administrative penalties plus outstanding contributions. Child labor: up to 3 months imprisonment.
exceptions: Agriculture workers and domestic workers have modified minimum wage rates under separate Wages Board orders
Family businesses employing only family members have modified registration requirements
Cooperatives have modified Social Security Fund contribution rules

quiz.q: What percentage of Nepal's workers operate in the informal economy beyond the Labor Act's practical reach?
options: About 20% — Nepal has largely formalized its workforce
About 50% — a significant but manageable informal sector
Over 90% — the vast majority of Nepali workers are in the informal economy
100% — Nepal has no formal employment sector
quiz.explanation: Nepal's informal economy employs over 90% of workers — subsistence farmers, rural artisans, domestic workers, street vendors, construction laborers hired daily. The formal sector (government, banks, major corporations) employing the remaining 10% has Labor Act protections, but most Nepalis work outside any enforceable labor protection framework. This informality means minimum wage, working hours, and social security laws exist primarily on paper for the majority of the workforce. Nepal's labor challenge is not writing better laws but creating an economy that generates formal employment.

laws.title: Human Trafficking and Transportation Control Act Nepal
laws.subtitle: Nepal's trafficking vulnerability and enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Nepal is a significant origin and transit country for human trafficking. Women and girls are trafficked to India for sexual exploitation (India's open border with Nepal facilitates trafficking), to Gulf countries as domestic workers under fraudulent contracts, and increasingly to China as brides for rural Chinese men facing gender imbalance from the one-child policy. Children are trafficked into circuses, domestic work, and bonded labor. Nepal's Human Trafficking and Transportation Control Act (2007) criminalizes trafficking with severe penalties. Vulnerability factors: poverty, natural disasters (post-2015 earthquake trafficking spiked), and discriminatory social structures (Dalit and indigenous women most vulnerable).
laws.penalty: Trafficking for sexual exploitation: 20 years imprisonment. Trafficking child: up to 20 years. Trafficking for organ removal: up to 20 years. Using trafficked person's services: 6 months to 2 years.
exceptions: Safe migration assistance by licensed foreign employment agencies is legal
UNHCR-assisted refugee resettlement involving international movement is not trafficking
Return and reintegration assistance by NGOs is explicitly protected under the Act

quiz.q: Why did human trafficking in Nepal spike immediately after the 2015 earthquake?
options: The earthquake destroyed the border controls that were preventing trafficking
Post-earthquake poverty and displacement created extreme vulnerability: traffickers posed as rescuers or employers offering earthquake relief work, deceiving desperate families
The earthquake killed all the traffickers, so trafficking actually decreased
The 2015 earthquake occurred in winter — trafficking was unaffected because it only occurs in summer
quiz.explanation: Nepal's 2015 earthquake (7.8 magnitude, 9,000 deaths, 500,000 homes destroyed) created mass vulnerability. Within weeks, trafficking networks exploited the chaos: men appeared in affected villages offering employment, educational opportunities, or help with reconstruction — and trafficked women, girls, and children. UNICEF, IOM, and Nepali NGOs documented significant trafficking increases in the months after the earthquake. Disaster contexts are known risk-multipliers for trafficking: family separation, economic desperation, disrupted oversight systems, and population movement all facilitate exploitation.

laws.title: Foreign Aid Dependence and Aid Effectiveness Nepal
laws.subtitle: Nepal's development finance and donor-dependent governance
laws.fullDescription: Nepal is one of the most aid-dependent countries in the world: foreign aid comprises 20-30% of total government spending. Major donors include India, China, USA, World Bank, Asian Development Bank, EU, Japan, and bilateral European donors. Aid coordination is challenging: Nepal has 50+ bilateral and multilateral aid relationships. India-China competition over Nepal's infrastructure is acute — the Belt and Road Initiative (China) competes with India's connectivity projects. Nepal's constitution (Article 51) states that foreign aid must align with national priorities, but donor conditionality sometimes shapes policy. The Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) compact ($500M from USA, 2022) was debated intensely about sovereignty implications before ratification.
laws.penalty: Misuse of foreign aid funds: criminal prosecution under Good Governance Act and CIAA jurisdiction. Aid project corruption: same as general corruption provisions. Unauthorized foreign aid receipt by non-government entities: regulation violation.
exceptions: INGO registration with Social Welfare Council required but INGOs may operate in most sectors
UN agencies operate under Host Country Agreement with modified regulations
Diplomatic project assistance (Japan Grant Aid, Indian development projects) governed by bilateral agreement

quiz.q: What geopolitical competition plays out through infrastructure aid to Nepal?
options: Nepal is so poor that no major powers compete for influence there
India and China actively compete for Nepal's loyalty through infrastructure projects — Nepal's geographic position between them makes it a strategic prize
Only China provides aid to Nepal — India does not compete
The US dominates Nepal's aid landscape to the exclusion of India and China
quiz.explanation: Nepal sits literally between India and China — the two Asian giants competing for regional influence. Both provide infrastructure aid: India funds roads, power lines, railways, and cultural connections (Hindu nationalist ties to Nepal's former Hindu Kingdom); China's BRI offers connectivity north to Tibet and south through Nepal to India. Nepal has tried to leverage this competition ('balance between China and India') for better terms. But Nepal is small (30M people), landlocked, and economically dependent on India — giving India enormous leverage. Nepal's geopolitical navigation between its two giant neighbors shapes all foreign and development policy.

laws.title: Right to Information Act Nepal & Transparency
laws.subtitle: Freedom of information in Nepal's democracy
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Right to Information Act (2007) established citizens' right to access government information. Nepal's press freedom has expanded significantly since the Maoist conflict period when both sides targeted journalists. RSF ranks Nepal 76th globally in press freedom (2023) — among South Asia's best. However, journalists face challenges: sedition charges, criminal defamation (a criminal offense in Nepal), and digital media harassment. Nepal's media landscape has 1,000+ newspapers, hundreds of radio stations, and growing online media. The Social Media and Online Information Management Directive (2023) raised concerns about digital censorship. Nepal's Constituent Assembly debates were notable for public openness.
laws.penalty: Denial of information by public body without grounds: administrative complaint and penalty. Criminal defamation (publishing false information): up to 2 years imprisonment. Information disclosure causing national security risk: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Cabinet deliberations are exempt from RTI for 30 years
Security matters affecting national defense exempt
Personal information of private individuals not held by government exempt

quiz.q: How does Nepal rank in regional press freedom, and what law concerns digital rights organizations?
options: Nepal ranks last in South Asia on press freedom — worse than Bangladesh or Pakistan
Nepal ranks relatively well (76th globally) in press freedom — among South Asia's best — though the 2023 Social Media Directive raised digital censorship concerns
Nepal has never had any press freedom — all media is state-owned
Nepal bans all foreign media to protect national sovereignty
quiz.explanation: Nepal ranks 76th globally in RSF's Press Freedom Index — better than India (161st), Bangladesh (163rd), Pakistan (150th), and Sri Lanka (135th). Nepal's democratic transition from monarchy and Maoist rule created a relatively free media environment with 1,000+ newspapers and hundreds of radio stations. However, Nepal's 2023 Social Media and Online Information Management Directive, which could require online platforms to register and remove content, raised concerns from digital rights organizations about government overreach into online expression.

laws.title: Special Economic Zone Act Nepal & FDI Challenges
laws.subtitle: Nepal's efforts to attract foreign investment in challenging environment
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Special Economic Zone Act (2016) and Investment Board Nepal (IBN) aim to attract foreign direct investment. Nepal offers significant investment potential: hydropower, tourism, herbal/pharmaceutical products, and transit trade between India and China. However, Nepal's FDI remains very low: $200-300M annually. Barriers to investment include: difficult terrain and inadequate infrastructure, bureaucratic complexity (30+ approvals for industrial projects), political instability, and labor regulations perceived as rigid. Nepal's hydropower projects attract the most FDI — international developers working with Indian and Chinese energy companies. India's Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) for Nepal hydropower are critical to viability of projects.
laws.penalty: Foreign investment without IBN registration: administrative fines and business closure. Profit repatriation without Reserve Bank approval: administrative penalties. Tax evasion by foreign investors: standard tax law penalties plus additional scrutiny.
exceptions: Tourism businesses up to $1M may use simplified investment registration
IT companies in incubation centers receive modified FDI registration
100% foreign ownership permitted in most manufacturing sectors in SEZs

quiz.q: Why does Nepal attract so little foreign direct investment despite significant natural advantages?
options: Nepal has no natural advantages for investment
Nepal's FDI is low because it is already economically self-sufficient — it doesn't need foreign investment
Bureaucratic complexity (30+ approvals), political instability, and inadequate infrastructure deter investment despite hydropower and tourism potential
Foreign investment is legally prohibited in Nepal except for hydropower
quiz.explanation: Nepal's investment climate challenges are documented: a 2019 World Bank report found Nepal required 30+ distinct government approvals for major industrial investments — a bureaucratic maze that deters investors who have simpler options. Political instability (12 PMs in 15 years) means each government reshuffles priorities and relationships. Road and electricity infrastructure is inadequate. Labor laws perceived as rigid. Combined with Nepal's landlocked geography, these factors result in FDI of only $200-300M annually — despite hydropower potential that could generate billions in export revenue annually.

laws.title: Biodiversity Conservation and Forest Act Nepal
laws.subtitle: Nepal's forest management and community forestry success
laws.fullDescription: Nepal's Forest Act and National Biodiversity Strategy govern forests covering 44% of Nepal's land area.
